The Yellow-banded snapper (Lutjanus adetii) attains a maximum recorded body length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] in total length, representing the upper bound of its growth trajectory in the coastal waters of the western Pacific. During the egg incubation phase, maintained at a stable 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], the embryo develops rapidly, with eclosion occurring after a brief period of approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days]. The larva that emerges from the transparent, yolk-laden egg weighs a mere 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture, a value consistent with the minute egg diameters characteristic of lutjanids. This initial wet weight reflects the modest energetic reserves contained within the fertilised ovum, which must sustain the yolk-sac larva through the lecithotrophic phase until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins.

Sexual maturation in Lutjanus adetii occurs at a notably smaller body size relative to its ultimate length, with puberty triggered when individuals reach a total length of 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm]. Field surveys have confirmed that the length at which the onset of gonadal activity is observed falls within a range of 28 to 40 cm in total length [Lp = of 28 to 40 cm in total length], a value that does not include the 52 cm mark sometimes recorded for exceptionally large specimens. At this pubertal size, the corresponding wet weight of the fish is approximately 235.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 235.5 grams], derived from the strong allometric relationship between length and mass in this species. These sub-adult individuals, having completed the larval-juvenile transition and subsequent benthic juvenile phase, begin vitellogenesis and spermiation onset as they approach this critical size threshold, marking their transition into the spawning adult segment of the population.

Reproductive output in the Yellow-banded snapper has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. When the ambient seawater is held at 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], a single gravid female can produce approximately 3,000,000 eggs over the course of an entire year [Ri = approximately 3,000,000 eggs over the course of an entire year], translating into a mean daily egg production of roughly 8,219 eggs per day. This maximum reproductive output was calculated for individuals exhibiting a kap value of 0.85, indicating a high fraction of available resources being directed toward reproductive effort. The spawning adult, reproductively active and iteroparous, releases pelagic eggs during multiple spawning events throughout the breeding season, with the annual fecundity reflecting both the clutch size per event and the frequency of those events across the warmer months.

The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult Lutjanus adetii has been estimated at 1910 grams [Wwi = 1910 grams], a figure derived from the length-weight conversion using the relationship 0.01413 times the total length raised to the power of 3.02. This asymptotic mass represents the maximum recorded body mass in adults from the Great Barrier Reef region and surrounding Coral Sea habitats, typically achieved once the fish has reached the full 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] in total length. The growth curve of this species shows a pronounced deceleration after the pubertal size is passed, with the majority of somatic mass gain occurring during the juvenile and early sub-adult stages. Older, reproductively active individuals channel most of their ingested energy into gametogenesis and spawning rather than further increases in body mass, a pattern common among iteroparous tropical reef fishes.

Longevity data for the Yellow-banded snapper indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 40 years [am = approximately 40 years] in the wild when measured at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C], a duration that places it among the longer-lived members of the Lutjanidae family. This 40-year lifespan (40 years) [am = 40 years] corresponds to roughly 14,600 days, although individual variation exists depending on local environmental conditions and predation pressure at a temperature of 25.9 °C [T = 25.9 °C]. The natural mortality that eventually claims these organisms is typically a result of senescence, with age-related death occurring after reproductive output has begun to decline in very old individuals. Compared to congeneric species such as Lutjanus stellatus, the Yellow-banded snapper exhibits a relatively slow pace of life, with the extended juvenile phase and late onset of sexual maturation balanced by a high maximum age across the entire biological lifespan.
